title: A mesh picture shows where the cells are, but not whether they are enough
summary: Mesh screenshots are evidence of effort, not of adequacy. Read them for where the resolution sits and where probe lines are placed, then ask for what the picture cannot show: cell counts, refinement ratio and the quantity that stopped changing.

Blue arrows enter on the left, red arrows leave on the right, and white circles mark two vertical probe lines and one short line in the narrow section.

read_the_figure.question: Is the grid adequate for the flow it is meant to resolve, and where has the resolution been spent?
read_the_figure.axes: No axes: a software screenshot. The domain is the 2D axisymmetric half-plane of the base-case geometry (flow left to right, axis along the bottom). Colour carries no data: green is simply the mesh lines drawn so close together that they merge.
look_at: Blue arrows on the left are the inlet; red arrows on the right are the outlet. These confirm the boundary types picked in the geometry drawing.

The white circles with crosses are the probe lines (line monitors). There are two vertical lines in the wide reactor and one short cluster in the narrow section. Grid-convergence is judged on profiles along them.
The grey bar at the lower left is the lance wall inside the narrow section.

In the 3D screenshot (figure 07) the cells are tetrahedra, visibly denser in the bend and in the final section and sparse in the straight middle; a hexagonal-pattern inset shows the honeycomb that has to be meshed. A 60 mm / 10 mm / 5 mm / 0.25 mm label repeats the honeycomb dimensions.
read_the_figure.proves: Only that a mesh exists, that boundaries are marked and that the probe lines are in sensible places. Adequacy comes from the numbers: the profile along a probe line must stop changing as the mesh is refined.
if_wrong: A profile that keeps changing between fine and finer meshes: the grid is not in the asymptotic range, so differences between cases (lance size, fuel) may be partly mesh error.
Cells stretched to high aspect ratio where the flow turns: numerical diffusion smears the shear layer after the step.
Fine cells everywhere: the study becomes too expensive, which is exactly what happens for the 3D honeycomb.
must_check: Cell counts for at least three meshes and a constant refinement ratio.
The quantity compared (velocity, temperature, species) and where (which probe line).
A cell-quality statement: skewness, aspect ratio and for walls the wall-adjacent cell size.
A refinement near the step and the lance tip, where gradients are largest.
The convergence criterion of the solver was met on each mesh; otherwise the comparison is meaningless.

terms.meaning: Cells arranged in a regular grid of rows and columns. Cheap and accurate in simple domains such as this 2D one.
Unstructured mesh of four-faced cells. Easy to generate in a complicated 3D shape such as a bend with a honeycomb, but needs more cells for the same accuracy.
Showing that an output of interest stops changing as the cells get smaller.
The factor by which the cell size is reduced between meshes, usually at least 1.3 and often 2.
The exponent p fitted to how the output changes over three meshes.
A standard way to turn the difference between two meshes into an error band, with a safety factor.
A line in the domain along which solution profiles are recorded for comparison between meshes.
Longest over shortest cell edge. Large values are fine where the solution varies slowly across the short direction and harmful elsewhere.

remember: A mesh picture is not a mesh study. The study is the profile that stops changing.
Use at least three meshes with a constant refinement ratio so that the order can be estimated.
Refine where gradients are largest: shear layers, steps, lance tips and walls.
The grid convergence index with a safety factor of 1.25 is the usual way to state a numerical error band for three meshes.
A converged mesh is no proof that the model is right: verification and validation answer different questions.

understand.title: Why probe lines
understand.text: One number such as a peak temperature can look converged by accident. A profile along a line shows whether the shape has settled. Two lines in the reactor catch both the near-step and the far-field behaviour.

understand.title: Why the 3D case is harder
understand.text: The 2D domain is a simple rectangle pair that a structured mesh fills exactly. The honeycomb adds roughly a hundred small channels with thin walls; tetrahedral cells must be smaller than the wall gap, so the cell count balloons. The project text records that the planned flame-anchoring study was dropped for this reason.

steps.title: The refinement ratio
steps.note: Each mesh has a characteristic cell size h. In a 2D axisymmetric mesh h scales as the inverse square root of the cell count: h is proportional to N to the power -1/2.

steps.title: Observed order from three meshes
steps.note: f1 is the finest mesh, f3 the coarsest, all at constant r. If the differences shrink by a factor r^p each time, the output is in the asymptotic range.

steps.title: Richardson extrapolation
steps.note: The estimate of the mesh-independent value, assuming the leading error term dominates.

steps.title: Grid convergence index
steps.note: The safety factor F_s is 1.25 when three meshes are used (Roache). The GCI is the error band, in percent, to quote with the fine-mesh result.

worked.title: GCI from three hypothetical meshes
worked.problem: A velocity on a probe line is 0.95, 0.98 and 0.99 (arbitrary units) on the coarse, medium and fine meshes, with r = 2. Find p, the extrapolated value and the fine-mesh GCI. (These numbers are illustrative; the study's values are not shown in the figure.)

worked.answer: p is about 1.6, the mesh-independent estimate is about 0.995 and the fine mesh carries a numerical error band of about 0.6 percent. Computed.

analyze.q: Cells in the 2D mesh are drawn so densely that individual cells cannot be seen. What can and cannot be judged from the screenshot?
analyze.hint: Think of what a reviewer would ask for next.

analyze.q: Why would a tetrahedral mesh need many more cells than a structured one for the same domain and accuracy?
analyze.hint: Think of the shape of the cells and the direction of the gradients.

analyze.q: The probe lines sit downstream of the step. What flow feature would a probe line in the narrow section pick up instead?
analyze.hint: Look at the lance and the inlet boundary.

evaluate.q: Is a mesh study on a 2D axisymmetric model enough to trust the 3D cold-flow model with the honeycomb?
evaluate.hint: The geometry, the cells and the physics all differ.

evaluate.q: The project reports that the 3D cold-flow runs did not converge. What does that say about drawing conclusions from the 3D mesh figure?
evaluate.hint: A mesh figure documents the grid, not the solution.

create: Write the table you would put next to this screenshot so that the study can be checked: the three meshes, their cell counts, the refinement ratio and the monitored quantity on each probe line.
Propose a local refinement for the honeycomb that keeps the cell count manageable, for example meshing one representative channel or porous-medium replacement, and say what physics you lose.

checks.q: What does a grid-convergence study show?
checks.hint: Think about what changes and what should not.
checks.answer: That an output of interest stops changing, within a stated band, as the mesh is refined. It shows numerical error is small, not that the model is physically right.

checks.q: Three meshes give 0.95, 0.98 and 0.99 with r = 2. What is the observed order?
checks.hint: Use the log of the ratio of differences.

checks.q: Which is the better place for a probe line: the straight middle of the reactor or just behind the step?
checks.answer: Behind the step, because shear layers and recirculation make the profile most sensitive to the mesh; the straight middle can look converged on a bad mesh.

checks.q: A report shows a beautiful mesh picture and a single mesh. Is that grid convergence?
checks.answer: No. At least three meshes with a constant ratio and a compared quantity are needed; a picture of one mesh shows only what was used.

checks.q: How would you present the study so a reader can verify it in one table?
checks.hint: Columns for the mesh, N, h, the quantity.
checks.answer: One row per mesh with cell count, characteristic size, the monitored value on each probe line, the observed order and the GCI.
